papers.title: Social Bias or Social Desirability? Comparing Factorial Survey Experiments for Humans and Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Factorial survey experiments are a survey method from the social sciences that uses descriptions of socially complex situation (``vignettes'') to elicit judgments such as social bias. They provide two major benefits: (a), they reduce the effect of social desirability inherent in self-reported social biases, and (b), they make it possible to separate the effects of multiple sociodemographic attributes. These aspects are also desiderata for the evaluation of social bias in LLMs, but are often ignored in social bias evaluations. In our study, we evaluate social bias in humans and eleven LLMs on the basis of four different English and German factorial survey experiments. Our results show that the LLMs mirror the human biases only partially and sometimes even invert them. We provide evidence that this is due to a fundamental difference in how humans and LLMs react to socially complex situations. While such vignettes reduce social desirability bias in humans, this is not the case for LLMs, where the alignment-induced tendency towards socially desirable responses carries over directly. We therefore caution against applying bias measurement techniques from the social sciences that were developed for human to measure attitudes and bias in LLMs.

papers.title: Beyond What Is Visible: Context-Aware Sentiment Across Online Communities Among Crisis Events
papers.abstract: Social media offers timely insight into disaster experiences, yet online communities may not represent those affected on the ground. Uneven participation can bias crisis information systems toward data-rich locations and obscure communities with fewer digital traces. We address this with an adaptive cross-community learning framework that combines text and aggregate mobility signals with socioeconomic and hazard-informed community representations, supplementing sparse local observations with evidence from structurally related cities. We evaluate the framework on the January 2025 Southern California wildfires and 2024 Hurricane Helene in Florida. The adaptive model achieves the highest F1-score in both cases (0.5923 and 0.7615), while augmentation has its strongest effect where original observations are limited. The framework also reveals finer cross-city community-level sentiment variation and stronger sentiment-mobility correspondence than text-only models, with relationships differing across disaster contexts. These findings support crisis systems that better account for context-dependent evidence and improve interpretation of underrepresented community signals.

papers.title: Generative AI Produces and Transmits Beauty Bias
papers.abstract: Societies reward people judged to be attractive by standards intertwined with gender and race. In this paper, we examine if and how generative AI may contribute to these dynamics. We audited 27 text-to-image generators released between 2022 and 2026 using simple prompts that never mention attractiveness or beauty, analyzing 51,300 generated faces and 160,196 photographs of real people across primary and supplementary comparisons. We used three automated measures and collected ratings from 550 human raters on a subset of images. Nearly all generators produced faces scoring above photographed faces under automated measures, and human raters judged the outputs of all 23 generators as significantly more attractive than photographed faces, even after correction for multiple comparisons. When focusing our analysis on gender, we find that 37% of female-prompted generated faces outscored the median professional fashion model. Across racial, ethnic, and national categories, groups associated with darker skin tones tended to receive lower attractiveness scores than groups associated with lighter skin tones. In a preregistered hiring simulation experiment (N = 570), exposure to AI-generated faces selected for high human-rated attractiveness lowered hireability and trustworthiness ratings and reduced interview advancement for an identical test set of candidates paired with photographs of real people; exposure to retouched photographs produced no such effect. Generative AI can reproduce racial hierarchies and gendered patterns of beauty and alter the context in which real people are judged.

papers.title: A misinformation playbook sharpens judgement without breeding cynicism
papers.abstract: Misinformation harms public health and democracy, and generative artificial intelligence now writes falsehoods as persuasive as people's. Defences range from fact-checking individual claims to training people to resist falsehoods. Yet many claims are too new to check, and interventions that teach doubt can reduce belief in truth too. We propose a defence that targets not the facts of each claim but the persuasion strategies that recur across them. Here we show that learning misinformation's persuasion playbook, mapped from 214,646 fact-checked claims in 51 languages, can sharpen human and machine judgement of claims they know little about, without making either more cynical about true claims. The playbook spans social influence, information manipulation and emotional appeals, combined around a core of fear, conspiracy and fabrication. Briefed with it, plus a reminder that persuasion is not proof of falsehood, a language model better distinguished true from machine-generated false claims about events after its training data. In a pre-registered experiment, the same briefing improved people's discernment of claims they reported as unfamiliar and left their belief in true claims unchanged. Averaged over all claims, the gain was not statistically significant. Because it targets what recurs, this defence need not wait for claim-specific fact-checks.

papers.title: Provable Compliance: A Protocol for Runtime Compliance Evidence and Transaction-Specific Decisioning
papers.abstract: Regulated institutions already perform onboarding, screening, monitoring, and review, but compliance evidence ages, and whether it supports a decision depends on the institution, product, subject, counterparty, transaction, jurisdiction, risk tier, and purpose. A relying party therefore often cannot obtain compact, attributable proof of which evidence, policy, authority, and transaction context were current when a decision was made, a gap that grows as authority is delegated to software agents and scheduled workflows. We describe ChainIT Provable Compliance, the compliance-side layer of the ChainIT Authority Protocol. Each sourced or institution-generated fact is represented as a separate Evidence Assertion VDT with provenance, freshness, confidence, permitted purpose, and privacy classification; a versioned Compliance Policy Profile selects the applicable rules; a Business Rules Engine returns deterministic, reason-coded predicate results; and the organization's configured Workflow Engine composes them into a signed, time-bounded Compliance Decision VDT for one reliance event. The decision contributes a single predicate, Compliance Decision Permits, to session-eligibility and transaction-policy decisions. It never independently authorizes payment: only a final Allow together with an exact transaction digest, atomic capacity reservation, and a single-use execution credential can commit value. The paper specifies point-of-reliance freshness, scoped propagation of evidence changes, decision states, evidence domains (AML, sanctions, PEP, background, identity, and licensing), the U.S. and FATF regulatory context as of August 2026, privacy and disclosure controls, and residual risks.

papers.title: Causal Value Attribution of Marketing Labels in LLM-Generated Ads: A Deconfounder Approach
papers.abstract: As AI-generated content becomes commoditized, economic value increasingly shifts from final artifacts to the upstream expertise used to specify inputs that steer LLM generation. Yet organizations lack methods for valuing this expertise and identifying which individual skills or configurations causally improve performance. This study examines generative marketing, where structured expert labels serve as skill primitives conditioning LLM-generated advertisements. Estimating their causal effects is difficult because outcomes reflect stochastic LLM mediation, high-dimensional label interactions, and multimodal confounding. This study proposes D-VAE (Deconfounder Variational Autoencoder), a counterfactual-inference framework integrating a multi-treatment deconfounder with causal representation learning. D-VAE recovers causally disentangled expert-labeling logic and derives PAC-based bounds on omitted-variable bias from single-treatment confounders. Applied to 29,177 foundation-makeup ad creatives, D-VAE outperforms state-of-the-art benchmarks. A field experiment shows that recommended configurations increase engagement by 32.7% and perform statistically indistinguishably from human experts, while a simulation study confirms causal attribution under complex confounding and treatment interactions. Overall, the study shifts value assessment from AI-generated products to skills, providing a foundation for pricing and optimizing AI-augmented skill portfolios.

papers.title: Same Person, Different Advice: Auditing LLM Financial Advice with Repeated Risk-Tolerance Responses
papers.abstract: AI financial advisers set a client's stock allocation largely from one stated-risk question, yet people do not answer it the same way twice: in a national US panel, 41% of households chose a different answer two years later, and in a laboratory retest a third of people moved two or more points on a 0-10 scale after six months. Seven large language models from five providers gave one-turn allocation advice for 800 real household profiles in which only the risk answer changed. The recommended stock share moved by 10 to 16 percentage points on average, and by 24 to 35 when the answer changed, against 0.6 to 4.2 points for the same prompt asked twice; in the laboratory retest the rating alone moved advice by 11 to 18 points. Without any note, the models respond to the answer about as strongly as when told that it is very reliable (less so for the two Claude models). If that instructed response is how each model maps attitude to advice, discounting the answer for its measured reliability, as classical test theory prescribes, would cut the swings by a factor of 2.4 to 3.3. The swing is largest for clients under 40. A note that the answer is noisy steadies some models, but shifts their weight to the client's age and pulls cautious clients towards a generic middle allocation: clients unwilling to take any risk are advised 22% stocks instead of 4%. Three extra money questions reduce the swing for some models, with no statistically detectable change relative to how much advice differs across people. In a scripted test, one clarifying question removes nearly all of the swing from an answer the client then corrects (33.5 points to 1.9 on average) while keeping the response to a change the client confirms. We argue that same-person retest audits should be a standard check for AI advisers, and that what to do with an unreliable answer is a question of client autonomy as well as of statistics.

papers.title: Can AI interview? Comparing AI-led to Human-led Chat Interviews
papers.abstract: Large language model chatbots have been proposed as AI-interviewers for collecting qualitative interview data at scale, potentially bridging social science's longstanding divide between the breadth of surveys and the depth of qualitative interviews. This paper provides the first direct empirical comparison of data quality in AI-led and human-led interviews. In a randomized experiment (N = 41), university students were interviewed via synchronous text chat by either trained non-expert interviewers or a locally hosted AI system; we evaluate exposure, specificity, and relevance. Median interview duration was similar across conditions, but AI-interviewers asked more than twice as many questions per interview and elicited roughly 65 percent more respondent text per interview. Per-question responses were longer with human interviewers, though not after multiple-testing correction; only AI-condition participants skipped questions. Responses were almost uniformly on-topic in both conditions; for specificity we detect no difference, but the design cannot exclude one of up to three quarters of a point. These results were obtained with a small, locally hosted open-weight model (7B parameters), which addresses concerns about data security, GDPR compliance, and scientific reproducibility. Our findings support the viability of AI-interviewing for large-N qualitative data collection.

papers.title: Regulating for an AI Commons: Adopting, sustaining, and defending people-first innovation trajectories
papers.abstract: Technological principles of openness, interoperability, and decentralization are integral to building an AI economy that is accountable to the public and truly responsive to local needs and constraints. However, Big Tech's firm control over essential elements of the stack (such as chips, cloud, models, data, and talent) limits valuable alternatives from reaching the scale necessary for sustained growth. Worse still, hyperscalers continue to enclose and extract value from publicly funded and volunteer-driven technologies without adequately distributing these returns. We see consolidated power within a few entities and "enshittification" of once-transformative innovations. Embedding ethical micro-level tools (like open data repositories or small-language models) into workflows is promising, but without a consistent innovation strategy, they also often end up perpetuating and being appropriated by the same exploitative trajectories. Instead, this whitepaper outlines a three-pillared holistic and intentional policy approach that i) actively pushes for the adoption of cooperative technologies in existing and emerging systems, ii) sets up collective institutional structures to sustain and maintain them in the long-term, and iii) introduces regulatory proposals that limit private entities from disempowering them through uncontrolled enclosure and extraction. Through desk research and purpose-specific case studies, we argue for the importance of such an approach in the Global South, where structural constraints around infrastructure, financing, and policy governance make it difficult for AI commons and cooperative AI tools to emerge and survive. The paper concludes with key open questions for campaigners, policy advocates, researchers, and grassroots organizers to consider and explore while working towards peoples' solidarity within and between Global South countries.

papers.title: Evaluating Predictor-Corrector Dependence in Hard-Constrained Climate Emulators
papers.abstract: Climate emulators often enforce physical constraints by correcting each state predicted by a neural network, but evaluating only the corrected forecast conflates predictor skill with the effect of the correction. We introduce an evaluation framework that separates these contributions by comparing corrected forecasts, pre-correction predictions along corrected trajectories, and autonomous rollouts with correction disabled. We further cross correction during training and inference to distinguish its immediate effect from how it shapes the learned predictor, and use matched nonphysical controls to test whether improvements are specific to the physical correction. In ACE2, correction substantially improves physical consistency. In a three-seed ACE2 pilot, models trained with correction produce less accurate uncorrected precipitation forecasts at short horizons than models trained without correction, but more accurate forecasts at 10 and 30 days. This contradicts our preregistered hypothesis that the deficit would grow with forecast horizon. In a separate nine-seed experiment, directly supervising the uncorrected output reverses its precipitation forecast deficit at 72 hours while maintaining the accuracy of corrected forecasts at 24 hours. In ConCerNet's heat-equation system, projection-trained models have higher uncorrected trajectory-based vector-field RMSE than models trained without projection, while restoring the physical projection recovers accuracy far more effectively than a matched nonphysical control. Together, these results show that hard corrections can reshape the predictors trained alongside them, creating dependencies that are not visible from corrected forecasts alone. Hard-constrained emulators should therefore be evaluated by separately measuring predictor accuracy, correction effects, and their interaction during training.

papers.title: GCAM-Gym: A Benchmark for Agent-Based Climate Policy Search
papers.abstract: Comparing climate-policy search methods requires accounting for differences in policy control, available observations, feedback timing, and simulator budgets. We introduce GCAM-Gym, a Gymnasium-compatible environment that supports full-policy evaluation and stepwise control through a common interface and exposes the components of the policy objective. We compare seven search and control systems in three settings: target attainment and cost, cost-temperature trade-offs, and one-step delayed feedback. Each system is evaluated with ten seeds per setting, for a total of 3,210 attempted GCAM evaluations. Four systems share a budget of 24 attempts per seed; among these, CMA-ES achieves the highest interquartile mean (IQM) of the best returns from completed policy evaluations in all three settings. We release the evaluation archive and analysis tools to reconstruct the reported comparisons without running GCAM.

papers.title: Water-Energy-Data nexus reveals sustainability gaps and priorities for AI infrastructure
papers.abstract: The rapid growth of artificial intelligence (AI) depends on interconnected water, energy, and data systems spanning infrastructure life cycles and diverse geographies, with the potential to intensify water and energy insecurity, exacerbate social inequities and lead to cascading sustainability issues globally. Yet assessments commonly examine them separately, limiting our understanding of where resource pressures arise, how they are transferred across space, and who bears their consequences. To address these challenges, we established a water-energy-data (WED) nexus framework that captures the spatial and life-cycle dependencies of AI infrastructure, and use large language models to synthesize 12,825 water- or energy-related studies across four resource-intensive AI infrastructure activities: mineral extraction, semiconductor manufacturing, data center operation and electronic-waste processing. The evidence map identifies a mismatch between the interconnected activities supporting AI infrastructure and boundaries used to assess them. Researchers assess operational energy more than water use and other indirect demands, while interactions across locations and life-cycle activities remain understudied. These gaps obscure how resource demands shift among infrastructure nodes and regions, and how data-enabled benefits compare with their underlying costs. The WED nexus provides a foundation for integrated assessment of spatially metacoupled systems, while the evidence map can inform priorities for managing the sustainability implications of the AI boom.

papers.title: Bridging the Language Gap in Scholarly Data II: Enhancing Gender Inference for Chinese Names
papers.abstract: Perceived gender inference from names is important for inclusive scientometrics research, yet existing methods perform poorly on non-Western scholars. We address this gap for Chinese names, which appear in two forms, Hanzi and Pinyin, its Romanized form (e.g., Zhang Wei, Li Na). In international bibliographic records, names are often available only in Pinyin. However, a single pinyin name can correspond to multiple distinct hanzi characters with different gender associations, so gender inference from Pinyin alone is intrinsically ambiguous. To address this, we first develop two hanzi models, a regression model that produces a continuous gender score from 0 (male) to 1 (female), and a classification model that outputs one of three labels (\em{male}, \em{neutral}, \em{female}). We train them on a sample of hanzi names from Chinese-language physics publications, rated by 11 native Chinese speakers. On this sample, the models achieve an RMSE of $0.09$ and an R$^2$ of $0.85$ (regression), and macro-AUC of $0.97$ and a Cohen's $\kappa$ of $0.81$ (classification), demonstrating high performance that is robust to class imbalance. For pinyin names, we propose a pipeline that aggregates hanzi predictions via transliteration and frequency weighting, together with an ambiguity score that flags names whose gender cannot be resolved from Pinyin alone. Benchmarked against three off-the-shelf tools (Namsor, GPT, and Claude), our models achieve the highest agreement with human annotations for both gender scores and gender labels, in both scripts. Applied to an independent sample of Chinese-named authors in APS journals, our models assign a gender to every name, whereas existing Pinyin-based methods leave between 20\% and 100\% of names unclassified. These findings demonstrate the importance of hanzi-level information for reliable gender inference of Chinese names. Code and data are publicly available.

papers.title: A Large Language Model LLM Approach to COVID-19 Fake News Detection
papers.abstract: Text classification is a widely studied problem in information retrieval and data mining, with applications ranging from healthcare diagnosis to the detection of COVID-19-related fake news. Social media platforms generate vast volumes of user-generated text, and the rapid spread of misinformation during the pandemic has made automated fake news detection an important task. In this study, we apply pretrained transformer-based transfer learning (TL) models and large language models (LLMs), namely BERT-base, ALBERT-base, XLM-RoBERTa-base, DistilBERT, GPT-2, XLNet, and T5, to the COVID-19 English Tweets dataset, which contains 6,420 tweets labeled as real or fake. To further improve performance, we apply six late-fusion optimization techniques: weighted fusion, particle swarm optimization (PSO) fusion, the Nelder-Mead algorithm, Powell's method, the Broyden-Fletcher-Goldfarb-Shanno (BFGS) algorithm, and trust-region constrained optimization. Models are evaluated using accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score, and confusion-matrix heatmaps are used to visualize the predictions of each model. GPT-2 achieved the best performance, with an accuracy of 0.9631, precision of 0.9612, recall of 0.9610, and F1-score of 0.9600, while Nelder-Mead fusion achieved the best result among the fusion methods with an accuracy of 0.9610. These results highlight the value of LLMs for COVID-19 fake news detection. We conclude by outlining future directions, including multiclass classification, multilingual datasets, and real-time social media streams.

papers.title: Risk and Refusal: Mechanisms of LLM Responses to Suicidal Ideation
papers.abstract: Refusal is a common safety mechanism in large language models (LLMs), yet in contexts of suicidal ideation (SI), refusing to engage can itself constitute a safety failure. We evaluate how eight instruction-tuned LLMs respond to SI and self-harm disclosures across three datasets, varying whether models are informed that a disclosure expresses SI and whether they receive a clinician-developed response protocol, and complement this with mechanistic analyses in six open-weight models. Our results reveal a nuanced relationship between refusal and response-level risk. At baseline, elevated risk in model responses is driven primarily by inattention to the disclosure, alongside refusal to engage. Mechanistic analyses suggest that models may refuse SI disclosures through the same direction that mediates their refusals of harmful requests. However, informing models of the SI context, or suppressing refusal directly, increases engagement without reliably lowering response risk, and may raise it. In contrast, the clinician-guided protocol consistently reduces response-level risk while also reducing refusal. Together, these analyses and ablations motivate the need for models that refuse only when warranted and engage in interactionally safe ways when users disclose SI.

papers.title: PersonaCUABench: Benchmarking Computer-Use Agents Serving Diverse Personas
papers.abstract: Computer-use agents (CUAs) are commonly evaluated against fixed task specifications, but users may omit requirements, add constraints, or require approval before consequential actions. Completing the benchmark instruction does not guarantee serving the person who asked. We introduce PersonaCUABench, which holds 74 tasks across 11 domains fixed and varies only who asks. A persona agent, playing one of 44 personas in four groups, rewrites each instruction in that user's own words and answers the CUA's questions, while the CUA sees only the dialogue, never the profile or the original instruction. Across nine backbones (3,330 runs), mean task completion falls by 36% relative to the original requests. The losses have two sources: in 59.9% of cells that lose points, the agent engages with what the user asked for and still gets it wrong, and 11.2% are stops the user requested that the checker scores as failures. Even when a persona request is fully completed, the user gives the top satisfaction rating in only 62.7% of cells, against 84.1% for the original requests. CUAs should therefore be evaluated not only on task completion but also on whether they meet the requirements and constraints users express. Code: https://github.com/MatrAIx-ai/PersonaCUABench. Project page: https://matraix.ai/research/persona-cua.html

papers.title: Graphlet-based Decentralized Finance Transaction Method Classification
papers.abstract: Decentralized Finance (DeFi) transactions involve complex interactions among accounts, smart contracts, and tokens. We investigate whether network topology can identify transaction methods that describe DeFi operations. We extract directed graphlet features to classify the 30 most frequent methods. Our results show that graphlet features complement event log counts in improving classification performance. Using SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP), we further derive model explanations that reveal method-specific graphlet structural patterns.

papers.title: Bad Diagnosis: Analyzing Consent and Data Collection Practices of Mobile Medical Apps
papers.abstract: Mobile health (mHealth) apps collect personally-identifiable information while handling uniquely sensitive medical data, ranging from mental health records to real-time glucose or heart rate monitoring -- yet they remain poorly understood at scale. We present the first comprehensive analysis of consent and data collection practices across 10,000+ mHealth apps on the Google Play Store, combining static analysis and privacy policy examination. We develop a rigorous operational definition to distinguish health apps from general wellness programs, and design a measurement framework to detect misuse of permissions and violations of consent. Our analyses reveal a troubling ecosystem: 69.15% of apps request at least one permission unrelated to their stated purpose, with over 52.9% apps requesting location data, and 50.5% and 34.9% apps requesting camera and microphone access, respectively -- despite no functional justification based on app descriptions and stated purposes. Most alarmingly, nearly 93% of apps fail to provide users with a consent form, directly violating regulatory requirements such as GDPR; and even among the remaining 7%, 1 in 14 demonstrate a gap between the obtained consent and collection of personally identifiable information. These findings demonstrate an urgent need for stronger enforcement of privacy regulations in mHealth apps. We plan to release our dataset and measurement tools for continued monitoring of this critical space.

papers.title: Harmful YouTube Video Detection: A Taxonomy of Online Harm and MLLMs as Alternative Annotators
papers.abstract: Video platforms, used by billions globally, are criticized for exposing users to harmful content. Yet, detecting online harm remains challenging due to inconsistent approaches to what constitutes harm and limitations of human annotation. We address both challenges. Theoretically, we integrate and expand existing taxonomies and platform guidelines to multimodal contexts and develop a comprehensive taxonomy for online harm. We categorize online harm on video platforms into six content-based categories: Information, Hate and harassment, Addictive, Clickbait, Sexual, and Physical harms. Methodologically, we propose and systematically test multimodal large language models (MLLMs) as alternative annotators of harmful videos. We curate a dataset of 19,422 potentially harmful YouTube videos and annotate them using GPT-4-Turbo, non-trained crowdworkers, and trained annotators. We discuss the potential applications of MLLMs in platform content moderation and social science research, particularly in contexts where they perform comparably to human annotators in binary and multi-label classification tasks.

papers.title: Board gender diversity and emissions performance: Insights from panel regressions, machine learning, and explainable AI
papers.abstract: With European Union initiatives mandating gender quotas on corporate boards, a key question arises: Is greater board gender diversity (BGD) associated with better emissions performance (EP)? To answer this question, we examine the influence of BGD on EP across a sample of European firms from 2016 to 2022. Using panel regressions, advanced machine learning algorithms, and explainable AI, we reveal a non-linear relationship. Specifically, EP improves with BGD up to an optimal level of approximately 35 %, beyond which further increases in BGD yield no additional improvement in EP. A minimum BGD threshold of 22 % is necessary for meaningful improvements in EP. To assess the legitimacy of EP outcomes, this study examines whether ESG controversies weaken the BGD-EP relationship. The results show no significant effect, suggesting that BGD's impact is driven by governance mechanisms rather than symbolic actions. Additionally, path analysis indicates that while environmental innovation contributes to EP, it is not the mediating channel through which BGD promotes EP. The results have implications for academics, businesses, and regulators.

papers.title: AI-exposed jobs deteriorated before ChatGPT
papers.abstract: Public debate links worsening job prospects for AI-exposed occupations to the release of ChatGPT in late 2022. Using monthly U.S. unemployment insurance records, we measure occupation- and location-specific unemployment risk and find that risk rose in AI-exposed occupations beginning in early 2022, months before ChatGPT was released. Analyzing millions of LinkedIn profiles, we show that graduate cohorts from 2021 onward entered AI-exposed jobs at lower rates than earlier cohorts, with gaps opening before late 2022. Finally, from millions of university syllabi, we find that graduates taking more LLM-exposed curricula had shorter job searches after ChatGPT and higher first-job pay when entering highly exposed occupations. Together, these results---pointing to forces pre-dating generative AI and to the ongoing value of LLM-relevant education---suggest that generative AI may not be the root cause of these labor market hardships and that the launch of ChatGPT is a faulty natural experiment for understanding AI's impact on jobs.

papers.title: Epistemological Debt: A Conceptual Framework for AI-Dependent Software Engineering
papers.abstract: This paper proposes a conceptual framework for Epistemological Debt, a liability that AI-dependent software engineering creates and conventional engineering metrics miss: the share of a system's behavior that no maintainer can currently explain. The debt accrues in two ways concurrently inside a single workforce. Maintainers with no theory of a system ship generated changes without forming one, and maintainers with a theory stop deriving changes themselves, so the system drifts away from a theory that is still intact. Neither is the attentional lapse the automation complacency literature describes, and the paper explains how to tell them apart. Against technical debt, tacit knowledge, and Naur's theory-building account, the contribution is this: both mechanisms share a cause, and running concurrently, they close the transfer window that earlier accounts of deskilling under automation relied on. The framework is stated as six propositions and two open hypotheses, with an evaluation design that separates the mechanism from the alternatives. Amazon's 2025 and 2026 service incidents illustrate the governance gap the framework predicts; that reading is labeled as interpretation. Proposed interventions are sorted into those that build comprehension and those that only limit risk; none is claimed as validated.

papers.title: Risk Ceilings and Development Deadlines: Pacing AI under Uncertain Safety Productivity
papers.abstract: Can a regulator promise both a risk ceiling and a development deadline when safety productivity is unknown? A ceiling below the final model's unprotected hazard requires a minimum stock of safety knowledge, so both promises hold only if weak research can be ruled out. Learning first and then replaying development, with spare compute in safety, comes close to that minimum. In a calibration with only state risk, constant safety yield, and full knowledge transfer, it needs only 3.3 percent more productivity than the necessary bound. Customer services pay for the guarantee. Rules that fix compute allocation fix dates, not risk.

papers.title: A null model to detect coordinated online behavior integrating evidence from multiple indicators
papers.abstract: Coordinated online accounts can amplify messages and manipulate attention, but detecting such behavior is challenging due to confounding factors like account activity and item popularity. We propose a statistical null-model framework that assesses behavioral similarity between accounts by comparing observed coordination indicators against activity- and popularity-conditioned reference distributions. By combining evidence across multiple indicators and partners, our method can identify suspicious coordination links more accurately. Evaluations on nine labeled information-operation datasets involving over 152 thousand accounts show that aggregating p-values multiplicatively across indicators and partners yields improved detection performance. While results vary across information operations, this approach offers a generalizable and statistically principled tool for uncovering coordinated online behavior.

papers.title: Generative artificial intelligence in fifth-generation education systems: A systematic review
papers.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence is increasingly transforming education by enabling adaptive learning environments, personalized instructional support, and collaborative knowledge creation, while also assisting research, assessment, and academic administration. In the context of fifth generation education systems, the integration of generative artificial intelligence offers new opportunities to enhance student engagement, support innovative pedagogical practices, and improve scholarly productivity. This study presents a systematic review of recent research on the adoption of generative artificial intelligence in primary, secondary, and higher education institutions, using established guidelines for systematic literature reviews and bibliometric analysis. The review examines applications of generative artificial intelligence for learners, educators, and researchers, and identifies key challenges including academic integrity risks, algorithmic bias, ethical concerns, data privacy issues, and unequal access to advanced educational technologies. By analyzing research trends, thematic relationships, and existing gaps, this study provides insights for the design of adaptive learning systems, the promotion of responsible use of artificial intelligence in education, and the direction of future research efforts. Overall, the findings highlight the potential of generative artificial intelligence to support human machine collaboration, lifelong learning, and inclusive educational environments, offering practical guidance for policymakers, educators, and engineers seeking to apply artificial intelligence for meaningful educational impact.

papers.title: Collaborating with AI Agents: Field Experiments on Teamwork, Productivity, and Performance
papers.abstract: We examined the mechanisms underlying productivity and performance gains from AI agents using a large-scale experiment on Pairit, a platform we developed to study human-AI collaboration. We randomly assigned 2,234 participants to human-human and human-AI teams that produced 11,024 ads. We evaluated the ads using independent human ratings and a field experiment on X which garnered ~5M impressions. We found human-AI teams produced 50% more ads per worker and higher text quality, while human-human teams produced higher image quality, suggesting a jagged frontier of AI agent capability. Human-AI teams also produced more homogeneous outputs (diversity collapse) as their ads were more self-similar. The field experiment revealed higher text quality (produced by human-AI teams) increased click-through rates and view time, while higher image quality (produced by human-human teams) improved cost-per-click rates. Two mechanisms explained these effects: Human-AI collaboration was significantly more task-oriented and displayed more delegation. AI-appropriate work processes, in turn, improved performance in human-AI teams and transcended the jagged frontier: Task-oriented communication produced higher productivity, higher quality ads across all dimensions, and displayed no diversity collapse in their outputs, while human-AI teams with more interpersonal communication were less productive and produced lower quality ads across all dimensions. In contrast, in human-human teams, interpersonal communication improved productivity. Delegation improved text quality in human-AI teams and was positively associated with diversity collapse, creating homogeneous outputs of higher average quality. The results suggest AI agents drive productivity, performance, and output diversity by reshaping teamwork along the jagged frontier of AI capabilities.

papers.title: Computational Multi-Agents Society Experiments: Social Modeling Framework Based on Generative Agents
papers.abstract: Computational social science has developed descriptive, interpretative, and predictive modeling, but comprehensive modeling combining in-world human intervention with outcome forecasting remains underexplored. Generative agent-based platforms scale populations or reproduce complex scenarios, but researchers typically act through setup, external controls, or post-hoc analysis rather than in-world roles. We introduce Computational Multi-Agent Society Experiments (CMASE), a generative agent-based framework for in-world researcher participation and traceable interventions at runtime. Treating simulation as a simulated ethnographic field, CMASE supports (1) real-time human-computer interaction to study intervention processes; (2) controlled experiments with ethnography-inspired observation, interviewing, and interpretation; and (3) forward exploration of intervention trajectories and downstream responses. CMASE combines LLM-driven perception, memory, and emotion; a composable environment built from texture and area maps; and researcher roles spanning observation, interviewing, participation, and intervention, so that interventions enter as social events rather than exogenous parameters. We replicate two published field studies from different disciplines: urban greenery and social fragmentation, and cooperation in a public goods game, using two substantially different language models. CMASE reproduces reported statistical patterns and provides process-level records for mechanism-oriented interpretation. A controlled comparison shows that embedded social interventions leave observable, auditable processes that parametric manipulation does not. These findings highlight CMASE's methodological value for studying interventions in small- and medium-scale social settings and its interdisciplinary potential. The official code is available at: https://github.com/armihia/CMASE.

papers.title: Pro-AI Bias in Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly employed for decision-support across multiple domains. We ask whether these models favor artificial intelligence (AI) itself. We examine this question through three experiments. First, in open-ended advice across investment, study, career, and startup domains, AI is prominent in most recommendation lists and is usually ranked first when it appears. Second, in salary estimations, models overestimate AI-related jobs more than they do for closely matched non-AI jobs. In a controlled follow-up, changing only the job title from the matched non-AI title to the AI-related title raises predicted salary by 10%, while all other supplied job details remain fixed. Finally, we show that the number of degrees and other credentials awarded by AI programs were 28% more overestimated than corresponding awards for matched computing programs. Overall, we show that AI is not only prominent in everyday LLM advice, but also receives systematically inflated quantitative estimates compared to non-AI cases, even against its closest disciplinary neighbors, raising concerns for high-stakes decision support.

papers.title: Happy Young Women, Grumpy Old Men? Emotion-Driven Demographic Biases in Synthetic Face Generation
papers.abstract: Synthetic faces from text-to-image (T2I) models pervade digital media, yet their demographic biases under emotionally conditioned prompts remain poorly understood. We aim to systematically audit how emotionally conditioned prompts affect demographic and perceived-attractiveness biases in synthetic faces generated by T2I models, with particular attention to intersectional patterns and cross-ecosystem differences across model families. We audited eight (4 Western and 4 Chinese) T2I models and generated 56,000 faces under seven prompt conditions: a neutral baseline and six emotion conditions. We quantified biases in gender, race, age, and perceived attractiveness using information-theoretic divergence metrics. We further conducted intersectional analyses across combined demographic attributes and compared patterns between the Western and Chinese model groups to assess cross-ecosystem consistency and divergence in bias behavior. All models show strong overrepresentation of young faces, and most also overrepresent White-coded individuals. Intersectional analysis reveals compound underrepresentation or near-erasure of specific demographic combinations, such as young x female x Black faces, which are largely absent across models and are not captured by single-attribute audits. Emotion prompts act as additional demographic selectors: negatively valenced emotions (including sadness and fear) consistently shift outputs toward White, middle-aged, male-coded faces. This produces a valence-driven mapping that is also associated with lower perceived attractiveness in generated faces. These findings indicate that demographic bias in T2I face generation is both pervasive and shaped by emotional conditioning. They underscore the need for intersectional, emotion-conditioned, and multilingual demographic audits as part of standard pre-deployment evaluation practices.

papers.title: Language Model Goal Selection Differs from Humans' in a Self-Directed Learning Task
papers.abstract: Whether in agentic workflows, social studies, or chat settings, large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being asked to replace humans in choosing which goals to pursue, rather than completing predefined tasks. However, the assumption that LLMs accurately reflect human preferences for goal setting remains largely untested. We assess the validity of LLMs as proxies for human goal selection in a controlled, self-directed learning task borrowed from cognitive science. Across five models (GPT-5, Gemini 2.5 Pro, Claude Sonnet 4.5, Qwen3 32B, and Centaur), we find substantial divergence from human behavior. While people gradually explore and learn to achieve goals with diversity across individuals, most models exploit a single identified solution or show surprisingly low performance, with distinct patterns across models and little variability across instances of the same model. Chain-of-thought reasoning and persona steering provide limited improvements, and our conclusions hold across experimental settings. While they await confirmation in applied settings, these findings highlight the uniqueness of human goal selection and caution against its replacement with current models.
